claim.why_it_matters: The zero indentation detaches sub-item b. (and the tail of sub-item a.) from their parent list item 1) b) 3. When rendered, b. becomes a top-level paragraph and the reader loses the fact that it is the second alternative of 'If the LAST phrase is specified one of the following occurs' - i.e. the condition under which the RAISING phrase is ignored. The transcription lost the nesting at the page break.

verdict.reasoning:
REFUTED - the difference is leading whitespace only, produced by a universal page-boundary convention, and no content is missing, altered, reordered, or misplaced.

1. WORD-FOR-WORD IDENTITY. I read the 300dpi render of spec_p663.png against specs/ISO_COBOL.md lines 27419 and 27421. Both blocks are transcribed verbatim. PDF: '3 exception for EC-USER and that exception condition is not specified in the RAISING phrase of the procedure division header of the source element in which this EXIT statement is contained, the EC-RAISING-NOT-SPECIFIED exception condition is set to exist in the activating runtime element instead of the EC-USER exception condition.' - the markdown matches exactly, including ISO's own defect ('this EXIT statement' inside the GOBACK section 14.9.18.4). PDF: 'b. If no exception condition is raised, the RAISING phrase is ignored and no exception condition is set to exist in the activating runtime element.' - the markdown matches exactly.

2. THE CHOICE INDICATOR IS NOT LOST. The claim is filed as a lost/detached list item, so I looked at the printed glyphs. In the PDF the marker 'b.' is set as a hanging label at x~335 (displayed coords) with its body text at x~378. The markdown preserves that marker literally: line 27421 begins 'b. If no exception condition is raised'. The letter 'b.' is present in both sources. Nothing that carries the a./b. alternation was dropped.

3. NO CONTENT IS MISPLACED. The kind is 'misplaced-content', but the ordering is identical in both sources: item 3. and sub-item a. end page 662 (md lines 27404, 27406), the continuation of a. and then sibling b. open page 663 (md lines 27419, 27421), then general rule 2) follows (md line 27423). Sub-item a. is the immediately preceding content block, three lines above b. in the same file. Nothing was moved to the wrong place.

4. THE TOP-OF-PAGE BLOCK IS A HYPHENATED CONTINUATION, WHICH IS ISO'S OWN PAGE BREAK. Page 662 ends '... If the exception condition is a level-' and page 663 opens '3 exception for EC-USER ...'. The word 'level-3' is split across the physical page break by ISO itself. In the PDF this block sits at x~380, i.e. aligned with the BODY-TEXT column of the a./b. level, confirming it is a wrapped continuation of a. rather than a new item. Note it reads '3 exception' with no period, so it cannot be confused with the '3.' marker on page 662. This is textbook hyphenation / page-break furniture, explicitly a reject condition.

5. THE DE-INDENT IS A UNIVERSAL TRANSCRIPTION CONVENTION, NOT A PAGE-663 DEFECT. I checked every page marker in the file: of 1233 pages, the first content line is at column 0 on 1233 of them and indented on 0. The indentation depth is unconditionally reset at every page start. I then scanned all single-lowercase-letter-plus-period markers: 37 are indented and 18 are at column 0, and the column-0 ones cluster at the very top of a page (lines 3658, 9845, 14326, 27421 and 35240 sit 0-1 content blocks after their page marker). Line 27421 is the second content block on page 663, so it is a straightforward instance of the same systemic reset - the transcriber does not re-establish nesting depth after a page break until a new recognizable top-level marker appears (here '2)' at line 27423). Filing this as a page-663-specific structural content finding mis-scopes a global formatting convention that affects all 1233 pages.

6. MEANING IS PRESERVED. A reader encounters, in order: '3. If the LAST phrase is specified one of the following occurs:', then 'a. If an exception condition is currently raised ...', then its continuation, then 'b. If no exception condition is raised ...'. The a./b. lettering sequence is intact and unambiguous. The normative content - that the RAISING phrase is ignored and no exception condition is set to exist in the activating runtime element when no exception condition is raised - is stated identically in both sources.

Per the rubric (reject when the difference is only page-break furniture, line wrapping, hyphenation, or formatting, and when meaning is unchanged), this is not a content discrepancy.
verdict.corrected_description: Not a content discrepancy. All text on page 663 is transcribed verbatim, in the correct order, with the 'b.' choice indicator preserved. The sole difference is leading whitespace: lines 27419 and 27421 sit at column 0 instead of the nine-space depth of their sibling 'a.' at line 27406. That de-indentation is a universal artifact of the transcription pipeline, which resets indentation at every page boundary - measured across the whole file, all 1233 page starts begin at column 0 and none are indented, and the column-0 letter markers cluster within 0-1 content blocks of a page start. Additionally the claim's line numbers are off by 3 (actual: 27419, 27421, 27406). If this behavior is to be tracked at all, it belongs in a single systemic ledger entry about page-boundary indentation loss covering the whole document, not as a structural misplaced-content finding against page 663.
